cells.tense: You are here, taking what is heavy, and it is not bending you out of shape.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Next time someone near you is in something hard, sit in it beside them and fix nothing — keep your own footing the whole way through.
cells.core:
You can take weight and not go rigid under it. That's the trick, and it's mostly yours already: what's heavy gets taken, and you stay someone who can set it down when the day is done. Where you're pointed matters. You steer by what you actually want, not by whatever is loudest, and that's why the load doesn't bend you.

The strain shows up in contact. Taking things well can turn into taking them alone, and alone is where strong starts to harden. So the next good move is small. When someone near you is in something hard, sit in it with them and fix nothing. Stay close while it's difficult. Keep your own footing the whole way through — that's the point. You can be near what they're carrying without lifting it off them, and what's already yours stays yours to set down.
cells.sheetLine: You take what's heavy without going hard.
cells.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
cells.place: Where you steer by what you actually want

cells.tense: You will be braced for something that hasn't happened yet, and doing it on purpose.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Look at one place where you're carrying more than your share. Set it right — one conversation, one clear change — then stop and touch it no further.
cells.core:
The strength that carries you is starting to grip. Somewhere ahead is a weight nobody has handed you yet, and you're already braced for it, gripped past what the moment calls for until the grip goes stiff. It looks like strength, and it works like a cage — mostly for the people standing near you.

Fairness is the fix, and it's something you can already do. Look at one place where you're carrying more than is yours and adjust the share until it's even, then stop. Not punishment, not a speech — a correction, then hands off. What it costs is this: you give up being the one who carries all of it. Do it once, plainly, and afterward let each side find its own level. The weight you brace against in advance is usually heavier than the weight itself.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for weight that hasn't landed yet.
cells.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
cells.place: Where you steer by what you actually want

cells.tense: Something got heavy, and you set it down before it could land on you.
cells.act: let go of the thing you are gripping
cells.ask: Find something you've been holding past the point it needed you. Put it down deliberately, not by dropping it, and keep your palms open for a day.
cells.core:
Under real pressure, bearing weight has stopped feeling possible. Not because you're weak — because at some point bearing anything started to read as danger, and stepping back became the safer move. What you steer by is still up there; you're just standing well back from the water. The want hasn't gone anywhere.

Trying harder won't fix this. Release is what returns, and release has a shape you can picture: put down on purpose what you've been gripping, and treat the setting down as a finishing, not a loss. Choose something, set it down clean — no spilling it on anyone on the way. Then keep your palms open a while. Not forever, just long enough to feel that empty isn't the same as gone. What refills you comes through the setting down, not the load.
cells.sheetLine: You set it down before it could land on you.
cells.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
cells.place: Where you steer by what you actually want

cells.tense: You keep taking things and call it nothing, while the room watches you do it.
cells.act: choose the light to steer by and turn toward it
cells.ask: Pick the thing in your life you'd be most wrecked to lose. Name it to yourself, once, and turn one degree toward it this week.
cells.core:
The strength is real and you don't count it. Under a weight that would bend most people, you keep standing, and if anyone described it back to you you'd credit the circumstance or say anyone would. You also don't see when you've folded under something. Both your standing and your folding go unwitnessed by the one doing them.

What's missing is smaller and simpler than strength: it's wanting. That instinct for what's genuinely good is already in you, pointed at the thing you'd be most wrecked to lose, and you rarely face it straight. Do that once, privately. No plan, no one told, no schedule. Just look at the thing, want it plainly with nobody watching, and turn a degree toward it. That small turn is the same strength, seen from your own side — the version of it that's yours to keep.
cells.sheetLine: Your strength works best when you're facing what you want.
cells.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
cells.place: Where you steer by what you actually want

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person's grip has already stiffened into rigidity — the record shows the capacity, not the history, so I describe the bracing as it happens in a moment and let them refuse it. A reader could reasonably say they hold on because people depend on them, not because holding has become a habit of its own; the ask survives that, since going back over three recent reaches and writing only the pattern teaches something either way. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you carry everyone' — cut, because it flatters the mechanism instead of describing it.
